pages.title: Jean Nouvel
pages.text:
Jean Nouvel (French: [ʒɑ̃ nuvɛl]; born 12 August 1945) is a French architect. Nouvel studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris and was a founding member of Mars 1976 and Syndicat de l'Architecture, France’s first labor union for architects. He has obtained a number of prestigious distinctions over the course of his career, including the Aga Khan Award for Architecture (for the Institut du Monde Arabe which Nouvel designed), the Wolf Prize in Arts in 2005 and the Pritzker Prize in 2008. A number of museums and architectural centres have presented retrospectives of his work.


== Family and education ==
Nouvel was born on 12 August 1945 in Fumel, France. He is the son of Renée and Roger Nouvel, who were teachers. When his father became the county's chief school superintendent, his family moved often. His parents encouraged Nouvel to study mathematics and language but when he was 16 years old he was captivated by art when a teacher taught him drawing. Although he later said he thought that his parents were guiding him to pursue a career in education or engineering, the family reached a compromise: he could study architecture, which they thought was less risky, as a profession, than art.
When Nouvel failed an entrance examination at the École des Beaux-Arts of Bordeaux, he moved to Paris, where he won first prize in a national competition to attend the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts. From 1967 to 1970, he earned his income as an assistant to architects Claude Parent and Paul Virilio, who, after only one year, made him a project manager in charge of building a large apartment complex.
Nouvel and the filmmaker Odile Fillion have two sons: Bertrand, a post-doctorate computer scientist working at Mindstorm Multitouch in London, and Pierre, a theater producer and designer at his company, Factoid. With his second wife, Catherine Richard, Nouvel has a daughter, Sarah. In 2008, He was living with Mia Hägg, a Swedish architect whose practice, Habiter Autrement (HA), is based in Paris. His third wife, Lida Guan, is a Chinese architect who worked with Nouvel.


== Practice ==

By age 25, Nouvel completed school and entered into his own partnership with François Seigneur. Early in his career, Nouvel became a key participant in intellectual debates about architecture in France: in 1976, he co-founded the Mars 1976 movement, a backlash against corporatism in architecture, and, a year later, the Syndicat de l'Architecture. For 15 years, he designed exhibits for the Biennale de Paris, where he made contacts in the arts and theater. Nouvel was one of the organizers of the competition for the rejuvenation of the Les Halles district (1977) and, in 1980, founded the first Paris architecture biennale.
In 1981, Nouvel, together with Architecture-Studio, won the design competition for the Institut du Monde Arabe (Arab World Institute) building in Paris, whose construction was completed in 1987 and brought Nouvel international fame. Mechanical lenses reminiscent of Arabic latticework in its south wall open and shut automatically, controlling interior lighting as the lenses' photoelectric cells respond to exterior light levels.
Nouvel had three different partners between 1972 and 1984: Gilbert Lezenes, Jean-François Guyot, and Pierre Soria. In 1985, with his junior architects Emmanuel Blamont, Jean-Marc Ibos and Mirto Vitart, he founded Jean Nouvel et Associés. Then, with Emmanuel Gattani, he formed JNEC in 1988. In 1994, he founded Ateliers Jean Nouvel, his present practice, with Michel Pélissié. Today, it is one of the largest architectural practices in France. Its main office in Paris employs 140 people. In addition, Ateliers Jean Nouvel has site offices in Rome, Geneva, Madrid, and Barcelona. The company is working on 30 active projects in 13 countries.

Nouvel has also designed products and furniture including cutlery for Georg Jensen in 2005, a flacon for a limited edition Yves Saint Laurent fragrance (L'Homme, 2008), and in 2012, the So So collection for American furniture manufacturer Emeco.


== Pritzker Prize ==

Nouvel was awarded the Pritzker Prize, architecture's highest honour, in 2008, for his work on more than 200 projects, among them, in the words of The New York Times, the "exotically louvered"  Arab World Institute, the bullet-shaped and "candy-colored" Torre Agbar in Barcelona, the "muscular" Guthrie Theater with its cantilevered bridge in Minneapolis, and in Paris, the "defiant, mysterious, and wildly eccentric" Musée du quai Branly (2006) and the Philharmonie de Paris (a "trip into the unknown" c. 2012).
Pritzker points to several more major works: in Europe, the Cartier Foundation for Contemporary Art (1994), the Culture and Convention Center in Lucerne (2000), the Opéra Nouvel in Lyon (1993), Expo 2002 in Switzerland and, under construction, the Copenhagen Concert Hall and the courthouse in Nantes (2000); as well as two tall towers in planning in North America, Tour Verre in New York City and a cancelled condominium tower in Los Angeles.
In its citation, the jury of the Pritzker prize noted:

Of the many phrases that might be used to describe the career of architect Jean Nouvel, foremost are those that emphasize his courageous pursuit of new ideas and his challenge of accepted norms in order to stretch the boundaries of the field. [...] The jury acknowledged the 'persistence, imagination, exuberance, and, above all, an insatiable urge for creative experimentation' as qualities abundant in Nouvel's work.


== Architectural style ==
In its biographical sketch of Nouvel, the Pritzker site quotes Bill Lacy's One Hundred Contemporary Architects: "Since the beginning of his architectural career in the 1970s, [Nouvel] has broken the aesthetic of modernism and post-modernism to create a stylistic language all his own. He places enormous importance on designing a building harmonious with its surroundings."
"I am often presented as an architect of ‘French high tech,’" Nouvel said, in a talk he gave in Milan in April 1995. "I would like to begin by explaining what I mean by the term modernity: Modernity is alive, it is not some historical movement that was interrupted a few decades ago.
Modernity is making the best use of our memory and moving ahead as fast as we can in terms of development."
Writing in The Architectural Review, Andrew Ayers quoted Nouvel's 1980 aperçu, "The future of architecture is no longer architectural," by which the architect meant that "rather than remaining a closed discipline, as it seemed to be in the technocratic France of the time, ‘architecture needed to seek its sources in the culture of today, in other disciplines’, and fully embrace the nature of the society of which it was the ultimate expression." Noting cinema's influence on Nouvel as well as the architect's affinity for postmodern philosophy, he added, "At its best, when [Nouvel] doesn’t overdo it, his is an approach that can enchant with its theatrical blurring of boundaries, its poetic feeling for atmosphere and its light-hearted play with signs and signifiers: the winking mechanical mashrabiyas of the Institut du Monde Arabe, the tree-filled mise en abyme of the crystalline Fondation Cartier, or the pluie de lumière that filters through the intricate metal-mesh dome of the Louvre Abu Dhabi."
"At his boldest, Nouvel is at the edge of what" the postmodern philosopher and media theorist Jean Baudrillard "called 'the sparkle and violence of American cities,'" wrote Amelia Stein, in The Guardian. "Both critics and admirers have commented that he eschews a formal language and, in a 2008 profile, the New York Times wrote that Nouvel’s work lacks even a 'readily apparent common sensibility.' 'They’re very right to say that,' Nouvel says, with quiet intensity, then a smile. 'I’m very proud of that. I’m not a painter or a writer; I don’t work in my room, I work in different cities with different people. I’m more akin to a movie-maker who makes movies on completely different subjects. To reduce style to the adoption of a formal language is such a short-sighted vision that if anybody is reproaching me for this, I would reproach their reproach.'”


== Projects ==

Nouvel has designed a number of notable buildings across the world, the most significant of which are listed below. As part of the announcement of Nouvel's Pritzker Prize, the Hyatt Foundation, which awards the prize, published a full illustrated list of Nouvel's architectural work, including projects which were never built, projects in construction, and designs for which construction has yet to start.
In 2001, the director Beat Kuert filmed a documentary about five of Nouvel's projects, titled Jean Nouvel.


=== Notable works ===
1987 – Nemausus 1 (Housing, 114 apartments), Nîmes, France
1987 – Arab World Institute (together with Architecture-Studio), Paris, France
1994 – Fondation Cartier pour l'Art Contemporain (Office / Cultural), Paris, France
1995 – Euralille, (Retail / Office / Housing), Lille, France
2000 – Culture and Convention Center (Performance Space / Conference Hall / Museum / Restaurant), Lucerne, Switzerland
2000 – Palais de Justice, Nantes, France
2001 – Golden Angel (Zlatý Anděl), Prague, Czech Republic
2002 – Monolith of Expo.02, Murten, Switzerland
2004 – Torre Agbar (Office), Barcelona, Spain
2004 – Museum Two, Leeum, Samsung Museum of Art, Seoul, South Korea
2005 – Reina Sofía Museum expansion, Madrid, Spain
2006 – Musée du quai Branly, Paris, France
2006 – Guthrie Theater, Minneapolis, MN, USA
2009 – Copenhagen Concert Hall, Copenhagen, Denmark
2010 – 100 Eleventh Avenue, Manhattan, NY, USA.
2010 – Serpentine Gallery temporary pavilion, London
2010 – One New Change, London
2011 – Tower 25 in Nicosia
2012 – Doha Tower skyscraper, Doha, Qatar
2012 – City Hall, Montpellier.
2015 – Philharmonie de Paris, Paris
2015 – Tour Bleue, Charleroi
2016 – Le Nouvel Residences, Kuala Lumpur
2017 – Louvre Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates
2018 – La Marseillaise, Marseille, France
2019 – National Museum of Qatar, Doha, Qatar
2019 – 53W53, Manhattan, NY, USA
2020 – Stelios Ioannou Learning Resource Center project for the University of Cyprus, Nicosia, Cyprus
2022 – Cidade Matarazzo Rosewood Hotel, São Paulo, Brazil


=== Under construction ===
The Sharaan resort in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to be carved into a sandstone hill in the AlUla desert.
The Central Park redevelopment plan in Sydney will see 11 new buildings in partnership with architects such as Norman Foster to recreate an abandoned brewery occupying almost four inner-city blocks. Nouvel's 120-meter One Central Park is his first project in Australia, and will feature a cantilevered mirror hanging over the central square off of the side of the building.


=== Proposed ===
Nouvel is one of the architects involved in the designing of the new Slussen in Stockholm.
In February 2008, Nouvel agreed to design a 45-story luxury condo tower in upscale Century City section of Los Angeles. The tower will be of modern design—it is designed to maximize views of the Los Angeles Country Club from the units and is opposed by both homeowners associations in Beverly Hills for the shadows it will cast on many small homes and its next door neighbor, Beverly Hills High School.


=== Abandoned projects ===
1989 – The Tour Sans Fins (Office/High-Rise) at La Défense, France, was never realized. Nouvel's winning design, proposed as Europe's tallest building in 1989, was to change ground up from granite, followed by aluminum, stainless steel and finally glass—"increasingly diaphanous before disappearing into the sky".
2003 – The Carnegie Science Center addition by Nouvel in Pittsburgh was never realized. Nouvel's winning design ended up being too expensive and Nouvel's contract was terminated by the Carnegie Science Center, citing a "dramatic difference between the budget for the project and the estimated cost."
On Tuesday 27 May 2008 Nouvel's design won the contest for the upcoming Tour Signal in La Défense.


== Awards and honors ==
Nouvel and the buildings which he designed have received a number of distinctions during his career, the most prestigious of which are listed below.


=== Individual distinctions ===
Honorary degrees from the University of Buenos Aires (1983), the Royal College of Art, London (2002) and the University of Naples (2002).
Honorary fellow of the American Institute of Architects (1993) and of the Royal Institute of British Architects (1995).
In 1997, Nouvel was named Commandeur de l'Ordre des Arts et des Lettres. He first joined the order in 1983. He is also Chevalier de la légion d'honneur.
2005 – Wolf Prize in Arts
2008 – Pritzker Prize


=== Distinctions for projects ===
1989 Aga Khan Award for Architecture for the Institut du Monde Arabe. In 1987, the building also won the Équerre d'Argent awarded yearly to the best building in France.
2010 Wallpaper* Magazine Design Award, Best new public house category for Copenhagen Concert Hall


=== Retrospectives ===
2001 – Centre Pompidou, Paris
2005 – Louisiana Museum of Modern Art


== References ==


== External links ==

pages.title: 2026 French student protests
pages.text:
Demonstrations and protests against poor economic and school conditions by workers and lycée (high school) students have taken place in France since September 2026. In early October, the protests developed into a nationwide mobilization involving students, teachers, parents, political organizations, the yellow vests and trade unions, with an estimated 550,000–800,000 people participating nationwide.
Labour movements emerged in mid-September in reaction to the cost-of-living, debt, housing and fuel crisis caused by the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab Strait, spearheaded by a newly revived yellow vests movement. Causes also included high inflation, economic stagnation, social inequality and unemployment, coupled with austerity measures and social spending cuts.
Soon after, teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, run-down buildings, and limited public investment in social programs and infrastructure sparked immense students protests nationwide. Students noted stress linked to the university application website Parcoursup and high temperatures in classrooms that reached up to 40 °C (104 °F) during the 2026 European heatwaves. Despite forming separately, the protest movements joined on 17 October, along with other unrelated movements. These demonstrations are considered to be part of a wider European unrest which includes protests in Belgium, Albania, Greece, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Austria, Ireland, Serbia and Germany.
The initial police response used a variety of forceful crowd-control weapons, resulting in serious injuries, including to children. Violent conflict between police and protestors have led to 6,800 arrests, most of them of minors. The French government has accused the far-left of stirring up the unrest for political gain. Protester leaders have argued the movement is a spontaneous showing of economic grievance.
The police response drew criticism from human rights organizations like Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the UN Human Rights Office. The government rejected accusations of police repression, with Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez maintaining that the response had been proportionate in almost all cases and that some protests had turned into riots.


== Background ==


=== Economic conditions ===
In 2026, France's economy faced an unprecedented series of shocks. No economic growth occurred since the new year, shrinking by 0.2% in the first quarter, stagnating in the second quarter, and unexpectedly suffering a 0.1% decline in the third quarter of 2026. 
At the end of June, the Institut national de la statistique et des études économiques (Insee) reported government debt as €3.596 trillion ($4.08 trillion), approximately 119% of GDP, almost double the EU limit of under 60% of GDP; it is the highest in French history and third highest in the eurozone. Despite the debt crisis, deficit remained above 5% of GDP, far exceeding the EU threshold of 3%. Public spending also stood at 57% of GDP. However, it was uncovered in October that 32% of the Ministry of National Education’s budget of €28.5 billion ($32 billion) was used toward paying pensions for retirees and not education. Demographic imbalance shifted the worker-to-retiree ratio to 0.94 workers per pensioner.
Inflation accelerated while wages struggled to keep up, reaching 3.1% year-on-year in September and 3.4% by early October 2026, the highest since January 2024. Due to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab Strait in the 2026 Iran war and Yemeni civil war, the price of diesel in France rose to €2.37 per liter ($2.72 per liter) in September, just 1c below its record high of €2.38. Accommodating for the high fuel prices contributed to rising inflation and cost-of-living in the country.
Unemployment, poverty, high rent prices and government spending cuts also have motivated protestors both in France and across Europe.


=== Study conditions and government budget ===
The protests came at the start of the school year and at the same time as a public-sector strike over the government's budget plans, which include €61 billion in new spending cuts. Students cited unfilled teaching posts, overcrowded classes, long timetables and deteriorating facilities among their grievances. A 17-year-old pupil at the Lycée Paul-Éluard in Saint-Denis described temporary toilets without water, rats and cockroaches in school, and temperatures ranging from −5 °C in winter to 40 °C in summer in temporary classrooms. Another pupil described rooms with too few tables, noting that teachers had explained their own discontent before the pupils decided to join them. Ryad Rani, president of the secondary-students' union Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL), cited a pupil who had gone seven months without a French teacher in a year with a French exam, and classes of 32 to 36 students. Pupils elsewhere told ICI of classes of 35.
The Créteil rectorat told Agence France-Presse that demands still varied by school: teachers not replaced, class size, heavy timetables, shortages of education assistants, nurses, social workers and managers, incidents between pupils and teachers left without follow-up, and deficient undergraduate admissions web portal "Parcoursup". France Info summarized what it was hearing from pupils as more resources, smaller classes, buildings in better condition, enough teachers and staff, and less stress from Parcoursup.


=== Previous protests ===
In autumn 1990, lycée students, many from working-class Paris suburbs, protested over safety, cleanliness, staffing and materials. The protests reached on the order of 100,000 people in Paris and about 150,000 nationwide. Education minister Lionel Jospin answered with an emergency plan and an increase in the education budget.
In early 2005, lycée students and their teachers mobilized against reforms to the education system made by François Fillon, and in particular against a reform of the baccalauréat that they believed would lead to greater inequalities in the value of diplomas from different schools. Between 15,000 and 40,000 students took part in the protests. Fillon backed down and announced a government amendment removing changes to the baccalauréat from the bill.
In spring 2018, opposition to the ORE law and to the new Parcoursup platform was formed mainly among university occupations. A scattering of lycée blockades took place. In the autumn, lycée students mobilized again, against Parcoursup and against Jean-Michel Blanquer's baccalauréat reform. On 11 December, hundreds of establishments were blocked or badly disrupted. Le Monde diplomatique later wrote that this map could not be explained only by the knock-on effect of the yellow vests protests, then at their height, but that the yellow vest movement was part of the context. Parcoursup was kept, with some adjustments, and the baccalauréat reform went ahead.


== Organization ==

The USL's national call, for 29 September, named four grievances: lack of teachers and staff, "dilapidated lycées", overloaded timetables and classes, and the stress caused by Parcoursup. Rani said classes sometimes held 32 to 35 pupils and asked protesters to remain peaceful. The union later called a second day on 1 October, an "act two", and a further day of action on 6 October. On RTL on 30 September, Rani said dialogue bodies run by the ministry had been "abandoned", and that it was for the minister to take the first step. Following their meeting with Education Minister Édouard Geffray on 2 October, student union leaders voiced their dissatisfaction with the government's response and called for the mobilization to continue. The USL announced further demonstrations for 6 October, with several trade-union confederations, including the General Confederation of Labour (CGT), announcing that they would join the action. Other supporting trade union confederations included the Workers' Force (FO), National Union of Autonomous Trade Unions (UNSA), French Democratic Confederation of Labour (CFDT), Solidaires, French Confederation of Christian Workers (CFTC), and the Confédération Paysanne. The teachers' unions Unitary Trade Union Federation (FSU) and National Union of Independent Colleges and High Schools (SNALC) called for strikes and supported the protests as well.
Other lycée student unions supporting student mobilization and protests included the National High School Student Movement, the Student Union, and the "Les Lycéens!" union.


=== Participating and supporting organizations ===

The Union syndicale lycéenne and Union étudiante called for joint mobilization by secondary-school and university students on 1 October. Reporting on the demonstrations that day, Le Monde described a heterogeneous movement involving students seeking improved educational conditions as well as people involved in confrontations. It also reported that some participants were not pupils of the schools outside which they gathered.
La France Insoumise (LFI) representatives attended demonstrations. Jean-Luc Mélenchon stated that the party supported nonviolent protest and has participated in protests on 24 October.
Muslim students of France (French: Étudiants musulmans de France, EMF) also supported the mobilization. According to Le Point, the association and its local branches circulated calls for action from 5 to 9 October, while its Belfort branch had joined a demonstration alongside secondary-school students on 1 October. The magazine reported that EMF cooperated with RED Jeunes, with which it had co-founded the anti-Islamophobia collective Génération EDR in March 2025.


=== Others ===
The yellow vests movement began in 2018 as a protest against fuel taxes and the rising cost of living and has since returned as a symbol for the 2026 protests. The demonstrations lacked a single organizational leadership, yet they gave voice to diverse forms of social discontent, with grievances including cost of living, education, public spending, social inequality, and political corruption.


== Timeline ==


=== Emergence of the protests ===
On 15 September, workers, including fishermen, police officers, farmers, construction workers, energy workers, medical workers, university staff and other groups participated in demonstrations. On 17 September, fishermen took their boats and blockaded two ports in Nice and Sète, obstructing maritime traffic. Others burned tires and wooden pallets on roads to petrol depots in Frontignan, preventing access. On social media, the 2018 yellow vests movement saw a resurgence, with messages calling for a general mobilization on 17 October being shared.
Soon after the beginning of the new school year in September, several issues with the school infrastructure prompted students in French Guiana to block the Felix Éboué high school in Cayenne, denouncing poor conditions. In Mayotte, parents together with teachers and students have been blocking access to the lycee of the North of Acoua since the end of August, a movement which was "largely ignored" by mass media in metropolitan France.
In metropolitan France, the mobilization began on 21 September at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, a commune in the suburbs of Paris. The day after a teachers' strike on 17 September against lack of resources and staff, pupils organized a protest. Pupils said they felt neglected by the Ministry of National Education and cited lack of resources and staff, overcrowded classes, and rooms short of tables.
An academic source and the USL later presented that mobilization as the start of the national movement.
Contemporaneous reports, including Le Monde and a 24 September account by actu.fr, dated the spreading movement to Monday 21 September at the same lycée, where several teaching posts were unfilled. The Créteil rectorate said on 24 September that demands still varied by school.
Through 25 September the spread stayed local. Actu.fr said about 10 lycées were affected by 24 September, mainly in Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne, and described a copycat effect on social networks. That morning, pupils tried to block the entrance of the Lycée Auguste-Blanqui in Saint-Ouen until late morning. An academy spokesperson told AFP there had been a gathering and material damage but no injuries. Police dispersed the crowd without incident.
On 25 September the Créteil rectorate said the movement was gaining momentum and counted "a good dozen" lycées blocked, above all in Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne. It said some mobilizations had produced crowds and material damage. The Versailles rectorate reported disruption at three of 62 lycées in Essonne and mobilizations at five of 65 in Hauts-de-Seine. Le Monde later wrote that about 60 Paris-region lycées were disrupted on 24 and 25 September, that about 12 percent of the 468 public lycées saw attempted blockades, and that around 10 were actually blocked. Rani told AFP that it had started at Saint-Exupéry and "spread very quickly", and cited shortages of education assistants, nurses and social workers.


=== 28–30 September ===
On 28 September, Lecornu said escalation would be "irresponsible" and wrote that fireworks, fires, and violence near high schools endangered pupils, staff, and police. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 164 people had been arrested that day, 180 schools were affected, and 12 security officers, 12 students, and three staff were injured.
On 29 September, the Education Ministry said about 400 of the roughly 3,700 lycées were disrupted. Nuñez told BFM TV that 440 people had been detained, most of them minors. CNN published photographs of police firing tear gas at the Lycée César-Baggio in Lille. In Saint-Denis, La France Insoumise (LFI) mayor Bally Bagayoko stood with pupils outside the Lycée Paul-Éluard. On BFM on 29 September he said that violence could, at a given moment, be legitimate. On 30 September, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure referred him to the Bobigny prosecutor, under article 40 of the French code of criminal procedure, for suspected provocation to commit an offence. On 1 October, Bagayoko told France Info that he stood by the remarks and called for de-escalation. Politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon wrote that the pupils were harmless, that the crackdown had a racist undertone, and that LFI activists should "step in" between pupils and police.
On 30 September, Nuñez said 625 people were detained, 83 police and gendarmes were wounded, and 356 schools were affected. He described projectiles, attempted arson, and what he called urban violence. Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 119 pupils and staff had been injured since the protests began. In Tours, a young person was hospitalized with head injuries.


=== 1 October ===
On 1 October, university students joined the blockades. The Union étudiante reported about 30 campus blockades, including Paris Cité, Sorbonne University, Strasbourg, Montpellier, Lyon, and Rennes. France Info added Sciences Po Rennes, the University of Rennes and the Université de Bretagne-Occidentale, and said students at the University of Montpellier Paul Valéry and Aix-Marseille University were mobilized. Police counts that morning were lower than the evening total: 340 actions and 169 blockades by mid-morning, according to franceinfo. The evening Interior Ministry figure was 1,027 lycées affected, 222 blockaded, and 1,949 arrests. The Guardian reported nearly 3,000 lycée students detained since the start, including the Thursday figure.
Lecornu held an interministerial crisis meeting and told ministers to cancel travel. His office said the violence made it nearly impossible to keep schools open safely, and that intelligence services described the movement as "an operation organized by LFI and its proxies on the far left". LFI coordinator Manuel Bompard said the government was "sinking into conspiracism" and called the mobilization spontaneous.
Geffray ordered remote classes in areas where damage or blockages made buildings unsafe, and said that slightly over 400 establishments would be closed on 2 October. That evening the Interior Ministry said prefects had banned demonstrations outside the closed lycées. Paris police prefect Patrice Faure banned gatherings at 13 closed Paris schools.


=== 2 October ===

About 400 of France's roughly 3,700 lycées were closed on the orders of the prefects, with many switching to distance learning. Every prefect banned gatherings outside lycées closed that day. In Paris, the prefect of police, Patrice Faure, banned gatherings around 13 named closed lycées.
By midday, the Ministry of National Education said 564 establishments "have been or are the subject of actions or disruptions since the start of the day". The Île-de-France region said 55 lycées were "the scene of violence, clashes and damage". Mobilization was widely reported to be lower than on 1 October, but fires, fireworks, and clashes continued.
On BFM TV that morning, Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 1,207 lycées had been disrupted or blockaded on Thursday, that more than 100 had suffered "severe damage" since the start of the week, and that 65 education staff had been injured, including 40 headteachers. He said a staff flat in a Lyon lycée had been ransacked by people from outside the school, repeated that the movement had been "taken hostage by ultra-violent groups", and told parents that "in the street, children are in danger". At 09:00, he met with education unions, the Union syndicale lycéenne, parents' groups, and elected members of the Conseil national de la vie lycéenne. After the meeting, SNES-FSU general secretary Sophie Vénétitay said there were still "no guarantees" and called a strike for the following Tuesday in support of the lycée demands. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin told prosecutors to seek parental civil liability so families would pay for damage caused by their children.
A bin fire spread to the façade of the lycée professionnel Gaston-Bachelard in the 13th arrondissement of Paris early in the morning; the entrance windows blew out, and the Brigade de sapeurs-pompiers de Paris extinguished the blaze at about 07:55. Firefighters also put out a fire at the gate of the lycée Léonard-de-Vinci in the 15th. BFM TV filmed the charred entrance door of the lycée Roger-Verlomme, also on the 15th; Le Figaro reported that the fire followed a firework aimed at the door, that several bicycles burned, and that firefighters arrived within about two minutes. Le Parisien reported fireworks outside the lycée professionnel Beaugrenelle on rue Saint-Charles and a pallet-and-bin fire that firefighters put out shortly before 09:00. An Île-de-France regional employee was injured and treated by firefighters at the lycée Molière in the 16th arrondissement. Around midday, a barricade of bins was burning at Place de la Nation, and police used tear gas. The Île-de-France region also listed a serious fire at the lycée Henri-Moissan in Meaux. RTL quoted the headteacher as saying the façade, entrance hall, part of the canteen and some boarding rooms had burned, and that the damage ran into millions of euros. France Télévisions authenticated images of a fire outside a school in Montigny-lès-Metz.

At the lycée Bougainville in Nantes, fireworks and burning bins met the morning opening; police and CRS cleared several blockade attempts around 08:00, and Le Figaro reported 10 arrests nearby, one of a youth carrying a metal bar. In Rennes, bin-and-barrier barricades blocked traffic near the lycée Jean-Macé from about 08:30, with further tensions at Émile-Zola and Joliot-Curie; Agence France-Presse reported a barricade and a Palestinian flag on a main road. In Quimper, police used tear gas to disperse a blockade of several hundred people at the lycée Chaptal.
In Lyon, fireworks around 10:00 led to tear gas in the Foch district beside the lycée Édouard-Herriot; 44 establishments in the Rhône were closed, and a crowd remained outside the still-open lycée Ampère. In the Bordeaux academy, 18 lycées were closed and about 6,000 pupils were reported mobilized in Bordeaux, Mérignac, Bègles, Langon and Libourne; the authorities reported five police officers, one firefighter and four pupils injured, and two teachers confronted at their schools. In the Drôme, Agence France-Presse reported nine arrests and a policewoman injured in the knee during an intervention at a Montélimar lycée and taken to hospital. In Metz, ICI Lorraine reported fireworks and tear gas at the lycée Fabert early in the morning, one arrest outside the school, and a bin fire at the lycée professionnel Léonard-de-Vinci in Montigny-lès-Metz that licked the building before firefighters put it out. Further clashes and at least one arrest were reported at midday at the entrance of the university campus.
In Évreux, several hundred people gathered outside the lycée Aristide-Briand from 08:00 onward. Paris-Normandie reported a washing machine set alight, gates forced, windows broken and repeated fireworks, and quoted prefect Xavier Delarue denouncing "urban violence". France 3 Normandie reported that Delarue said groups had tried to force the entrance in order to burn the lycée, with Molotov cocktails and projectiles, and that the headteacher of another Évreux lycée said Aristide-Briand had suffered fireworks being used as projectiles and an intrusion that succeeded.
In La Ciotat, the local site Var Actu reported that a physics teacher at the lycée de la Méditerranée was hit in the face with the contents of a bottle described as containing petrol, briefly blinded, and then kicked, after he tried to put out a fire lit near a tree at about 08:25. It said the suspected teenager was caught and arrested. A live blog citing Le Figaro described the victim as the headteacher, "doused with petrol and beaten" while trying to calm a tense blockade.
A Friday claim that staff at the lycée Victor-Hugo in Marseille, beside Gare Saint-Charles, had been doused with petrol refers to Thursday 1 October, not a new attack. Franceinfo reported on 2 October that the lycée was closed after Thursday's clashes, that the entrance door was charred, and that the management team had been splashed with petrol. La Provence reported the rectorat's correction: the headteachers "were not directly targeted by youths who doused them" but were splashed while people poured petrol into bins. The Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region had said a headteacher, a deputy head, a general secretary and a team leader were attacked and doused. BFM Marseille reported that the prefecture and the rectorat said they would file a complaint, and that the damaged door had to be made safe.
Separately on 2 October, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said images of "rare violence" showed a police officer in Belfort deliberately targeted, thrown to the ground and beaten, including to the head, by masked people in black on the margins of the lycée blockades. The officer lost consciousness and was hospitalized; Nuñez said his condition was no longer a major concern. The Belfort prosecutor opened an investigation for attempted murder of a person holding public authority. France Info's photograph of the intervention is dated 1 October, so the beating itself may predate the Friday announcement.
No national arrest totals for 2 October had been published by early afternoon. The latest Interior Ministry count remained Thursday's: 1,949 arrests, with 305 police and gendarmes injured that day, and 1,793 people placed in custody since Monday, about 90 percent of them minors.


=== 5 October ===
On 5 October, 400 to 500 schools across France were partially or totally closed. Geffray said lessons were "totally or partly suspended" because security conditions "have not been fulfilled". He added that 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the protests began.
During the high-school mobilization, the Lycée des métiers Nicolas-Louis-Vauquelin in Paris's 13th arrondissement was targeted by a group of about ten youths wearing hoods, masks and black clothing. According to the head teacher, Carole Zerbib, and several pupils, the masked youths were not students at the school. It was the first call to blockade the school since the movement began.
Shortly before 8:00 a.m., as pupils were entering, fireworks were fired and a first fire was started in front of the metal door. Staff put that fire out. About 100 pupils were confined inside and moved upstairs. The group piled bins, bulky rubbish and bicycles against the entrance, brought over a sofa, smashed windows and tried to force the door, which held. After police and firefighters had left, the group returned around 9:00 a.m. and started two further fires at the doors with a flammable liquid, feeding them with the debris. Staff tried to extinguish the flames from inside, through the letter slot, and failed. Firefighters put out the last fire around 9:30 a.m. Pupils were evacuated shortly before 10:00 a.m. and sent home. The Paris education authority reported three fire starts, told parents not to come near the school, and classes were cancelled for the day.
At about 10:30 or 11:00 a.m. in Lens, outside the Lycée professionnel Auguste-Béhal, a 15-year-old pupil in seconde had his hand blown off by a police stun grenade during a blockade. Between 200 and 250 young people were gathered, and the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch, said some of them had thrown projectiles at police. Lauch and the prosecutor of Béthune, Étienne Thieffry, confirmed the injury, said the boy was taken to hospital in Lille, and said his life was not in danger. The IGPN was seized. A police source told Le Figaro that he had picked up a  dispersal grenade thrown by the CRS in order to throw it back, and that it exploded in his hand. The authorities said the exact circumstances still had to be established.


=== 6 October ===
On 6 October, the third nationwide day of mobilization began, with high school students and university students joining demonstrations and blockades across France. Several high schools and university campuses were blocked from early morning, including the Sorbonne in Paris, while dozens of demonstrations were expected across the country. In Lyon, police dispersed masked people who had blocked a tramway, with early clashes reported. The mobilization was also joined by education-sector and labour organizations, including the CGT. Fabien Roussel, national secretary of the French Communist Party (PCF), proposed the "Youth Plan 2027–2032" at a press conference (shortly before he left to join students on the streets), which, among many measures, included monetary contributions to hiring teachers and improving school infrastructure, decreasing school hours contributing to stress, and strengthening student democracy. Also attending were leaders of the Union of Communist Students and the Mouvement Jeunes Communistes de France.
Also, Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis was seen shielding student protesters from riot police that were deploying tear gas into the crowd. He was later seen with other members of his team being administered eye drops due to them being gassed. He received mixed reactions for this act, public figures like Victor Wembanyama praised the acts of Bally Bagayoko, and the students; others, like Fox News, alleged that he was further inciting violence, and spreading communism and propaganda.
Teachers and parents participated in the movement. The High School Students Union stated that around 1,800 high schools were either blockaded or would close for the day, and protests were reported in Marseille, Nantes, and Lyon, where the demonstrations started peacefully.


=== 7 October ===
Iran's ambassador was summoned to the French foreign ministry over what the latter described as a "disinformation campaign" conducted by official accounts of the Iranian foreign ministry. The rebuke came after Iran accused France of "extensive and flagrant human rights violations" by police and security forces during the protests.


=== 8 October ===
On 8 October, the student movement held a fourth nationwide day of action. The Interior Ministry counted 71,500 participants at marches, including 24,500 in Paris. A further 55,000 young people took part in demonstrations outside schools, according to the report. Student and university organizations called a fifth day of action for 13 October.


=== 13 October ===
For the fifth nationwide day of action, the Interior Ministry counted 161,500 participants nationally, while the youth inter-union estimated 480,000; the ministry counted 41,500 people in two Paris marches. Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg visited demonstrators outside Lycée Paul-Éluard in Saint-Denis. The Education Ministry said 214 schools were closed. Education Minister Édouard Geffray said the deployment of 3,000 substitute teachers to the most affected schools had begun.


=== 16 October ===
By 16 October, Geffray said around 160 schools remained blocked, while he described roughly one-third of the 3,700 lycées as having been significantly disrupted during the movement. Student activists said the start of school holidays would remove blockades as a tactic, and planned to hold assemblies during the break.


=== 17 October ===

On 17 October, protests escalated as student organizations joined nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and fuel prices, called by trade unions and the yellow vests movement. The protests brought together a wide array of groups—former Yellow vest members, climate campaigners, trade unionists, students protesters, and farmers. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 110 marches drew 550,000 participants, including 110,000 in Paris; organizers estimated 800,000. The Associated Press reported about 400 arrests during the day. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu later said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers and gendarmes injured.
